national.title: Ukraine says Starlink still restricted after Trump says limits lifted
national.summary: Issues remain with the network used by the Ukrainian military, sources say, after repeated denials of a deliberate slowdown.
national.body:
Ukraine is still recording issues with the Starlink network, sources within the defence ministry say, after Donald Trump said limits on the satellite uplink had been reversed by Elon Musk.

The sources told the BBC that instances of drones experiencing connection loss at speeds of 161km/h (100mph) were being recorded, hampering military operations.

The US president had denied instructing the tech billionaire to restrict connectivity to Starlink's military-grade counterpart, Starshield, before saying on Thursday that Musk had "put it back".

Musk previously said he was not behind the slowdown, which affected Ukraine's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations.

The Ukrainian defence ministry sources said the military was constantly monitoring the performance of both the Starlink and Starshield networks.

They added that there was "currently no confirmation that these restrictions have been lifted".

Last week, Kyiv said uplink speeds to the low Earth orbit satellites had been restricted, affecting the speed at which drones could travel. Any drone travelling faster than 100mph lost its connection, officials said.

Shortly after, Musk said that Starshield , which Ukraine uses for some of its operation, was controlled by the US military and suggested that the Pentagon could be behind the issues.

national.title: Girl accused of helping Russia kill Ukrainian soldiers with poison
national.summary: After receiving packages with "free drugs," the soldiers were "instructed to take them on camera," police said.
national.body: Ukrainian police said Friday they had detained a 17-year-old girl suspected of helping Russia's security services to poison Ukrainian soldiers and that two had died. Ukraine and Russia have throughout their war since 2022 accused each other of recruiting minors for sabotage acts including poisoning. The girl, who was not named, is suspected of having packaged deadly drugs and sending them to Ukrainian soldiers she contacted by Telegram, police said in a statement. She was arrested by police in Zhytomyr, west of Kyiv, after allegedly following instructions from a Russian handler in exchange for at least 5,000 hryvnias ($111), they said. After receiving packages with "free drugs," the soldiers were "instructed to take them on camera," the statement said. "The recipients did not know that the capsules contained a lethal dose of methadone," it said, adding that "two soldiers died from poisoning in the Zhytomyr region." Police said they had identified other recipients of the packages, which "prevented four more murders" across the country. "The young woman was notified that she is suspected of aiding and abetting the premeditated murder of two people as part of a prior conspiracy," the police statement said. She was also suspected of "shipping drugs and psychotropic substances for the purpose of distribution," it said, adding that she faced up to 15 years in jail if found guilty. Police cautioned that Russia aims "to kill our people and destabilize the situation within the country." "Do not accept medication or other substances, as well as food or drinks of dubious origin, from people you do not know well," police cautioned. national.title: Horse-drawn carriage ban approved by NYC Council
national.summary: The New York City Council voted Thursday on Romanch's Law, which will ban horse-drawn carriage rides in the city by 2028.
national.body: The New York City Council passed a bill banning horse-drawn carriage rides in the city by 2028.Lawmakers voted Thursday afternoon on Romanch's Law. The legislation is named after Romanch Mahajan, 18, who died during a carriage accident in June in Central Park."We want to make sure Romanch's death was not in vain," Saggar Chadha, the attorney for Romanch's family said. "Not just for Romanch, but so no one else is killed or injured by horse-drawn carriages in New York City."The bill is now headed to Mayor Zohran Mamdani to sign. "The mayor will sign this bill, and the Mamdani administration is working every day to ensure we can do so while providing the strongest possible protections for the owners and workers in this industry," Mamdani's office said in a statement to CBS News New York on Thursday night."With a majority of the Council behind us, we have a historic opportunity to protect New Yorkers, visitors, workers, and animals, and we intend to finish the job," council member Christopher Marte said prior to the vote.The bill is making history, as the carriages have been part of the park since its inception more than 160 years ago. It's ending operations in June 2028, with a transition plan for workers and owners required in 2027. The bill also calls for the humane placement of animals. Carriage owners and their families are arguing, however, that the plan doesn't go far enough. They rallied outside City Hall Wednesday and Thursday to push back. One family said they have spent nearly a century building their business. "I invested $400,000 two years ago to expand my father's dream, and you're coming here to steal it," owner Francesco Riccobono said."We are asking for fairness. We are asking for compassion. national.summary: This is President Peter Mutharika's fifth visit to South Africa this year.
national.body:
Malawi's opposition has demanded an explanation for President Peter Mutharika's prolonged stay in South Africa, as the country struggles with fuel shortages, power cuts and economic difficulties.

The 86-year-old Mutharika left Malawi on 6 October, for what officials described as a private visit. This is his fifth visit this year, with limited information made public on each of these trips.

"Malawi is at a critical moment, and there is a need for decisive action," the opposition Malawi Congress Party (MCP) said.

Information Minister Shadric Namalomba has denied that Mutharika's absence had created a leadership vacuum.

The professor who beat fraud allegations to become Malawi's president…again

Published 25 September 2025 Mutharika returned to power in October last year after defeating then-president Lazarus Chakwera.

His latest absence comes amid growing public scrutiny of his frequent visits to South Africa.

On Thursday, MCP campaign director Moses Kunkuyu told journalists in the capital, Lilongwe, that the opposition was not questioning the president's right to travel for personal reasons but wanted Vice-President Jane Ansah to address the nation over the country's mounting challenges.

national.title: Five Israelis wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed in West Bank shooting
national.summary: The attack comes at a time of heightened tensions in the West Bank and four days before Israel's general election.
national.body:
Five Israelis have been wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed by Israeli security forces following a shooting in the occupied West Bank, Israeli officials say.

Footage verified by the BBC shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen, at a military checkpoint at the entrance to the city of Hebron.

In response, Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had ordered the military to prepare for a full lockdown of the West Bank, beginning later on Friday.

The attack comes at a time of high tensions, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days time.

The two injured Israelis are in critical condition, according to Israel's ambulance service.

The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle. The military said they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there.

Unverified CCTV footage shows two gunmen exit a car armed with what appears to be a handgun and an assault rifle and start firing on soldiers at the checkpoint, before coming under return fire.

The Israeli military said it had begun raids on the homes of the attackers, while far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said he had ordered the demolition of several Palestinian buildings adjacent to the site of the attack.

national.title: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC finds
national.summary: The UN human rights chief Volker Türk says the multiple attacks may amount to war crimes.
national.body:
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.

UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.

The health minister of the group's civilian-affiliated government dismissed the allegations as propaganda.

Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud said it was a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.

Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.

Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.

The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.

"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.

national.title: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich
national.summary: Questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers, were raised earlier this month.
national.body:
Police in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial affairs of Roman Abramovich, following revelations by BBC Panorama that accountancy firm Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax.

Serious questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers were raised earlier this month in a joint report from the BBC and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ).

A Cypriot Ministry of Justice official told MPs this week that the report's findings would be looked at as part of a new investigation by the police's Financial Intelligence Unit.

Lawyers for Abramovich have said that he denies evading tax or concealing his fortune. Deloitte Cyprus said it acts "in compliance with applicable laws".

The police investigation was announced at a parliamentary committee meeting in the Cypriot capital, Nicosia, held to discuss the combating and prevention of money laundering.

The Ministry of Justice official told MPs the police would try to determine whether any criminal acts had been committed.

Last week, the report from the BBC and TBIJ detailed how accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus in 2006 meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.

Deloitte, which is the world's largest accountancy firm, also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth, through the falsification of documents.

national.title: Woman with Ebola in Nigeria confirmed as wife of Swiss diplomat
national.summary: Her husband is currently in isolation but has not developed any symptoms, Swiss officials say.
national.body:
Switzerland's foreign ministry has confirmed that the woman who has tested positive for Ebola in Nigeria is the wife of a Swiss diplomat.

The woman, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born national who lives in the Nigerian capital, Abuja, tested positive for the virus on 20 October, becoming the country's first confirmed Ebola patient in more than a decade.

They both travelled to Uganda earlier this month. Her husband is currently in isolation but has not developed any symptoms, according to the Swiss foreign ministry.

The ministry told the BBC that all 25 staff at its embassy in Nigeria were in good health and did not need to isolate.

The ministry said the woman had spent about a week at a private clinic in Abuja with symptoms before her diagnosis.

It believes she contracted the virus while travelling in Uganda, although health authorities have yet to establish the source of her infection.

Uganda borders Democratic Republic of Congo, where some 4,600 have died in the country's most deadly outbreak of Ebola. Two people died in Uganda shortly after the outbreak began in May but it has been declared free of Ebola since August.

The ministry said the decision not to isolate the embassy's eight Swiss and 17 local employees was taken in consultation with Nigeria's Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization (WHO).

HEBRON, West Bank — Israeli soldiers shot and killed two men who the military said had launched an attack near the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank on Friday morning. At least five people were injured, including some critically.

It did not elaborate on the target of the alleged attack. There was also no word on the identities of the two dead and those injured.

A few hours later, Israel ordered the army to prepare for a full closure of the West Bank. The office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said it instructed security forces to immediately cordon off the city of Hebron and prepare to fully close all of the West Bank, starting Friday.

The deadly shooting comes as Israeli voters will decide next Tuesday whether to grant Netanyahu yet another term as prime minister — or usher in a new era of Israeli politics. The election comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza.

Israel's government has warned of potential attacks by the country's "enemies" in the lead-up to the election.

Following the shooting, Netanyahu held an emergency meeting of his Security Cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies. He blamed Hamas, saying the militant group was "planning a major attack aimed at murdering innocent civilians."

"Our brave soldiers thwarted this attack with courage and determination," he said, without elaborating on what the planned attack entailed.

national.title: Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70 percent of websites
national.summary: Governments around the world are rushing to implement safety measures after AI technology found 'severe' vulnerabilities in a key programming language called PHP.
national.body:
A few months ago AI caused global alarm after autonomous agents were found to have cheated on evaluations and then tried to cover it up, in what became known as the "Hugging Face hack."

Understanding AI The AI safety debate is confusing. Here's our guide to the different factions This week, AI and hacking are back in the spotlight with AI technology credited to have helped prevent a global cybersecurity crisis.

Cyber-security firm Wiz Research, using OpenAI technology, announced on Wednesday it had discovered security flaws in a computer programming language that helps run some 70 percent of the world's websites.

OpenAI called the bug "one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory." Wiz Research warned that its "successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them."

Corporations and governments from the U.K. to Japan are now rushing to prevent hackers from capitalizing on the flaws.

The flaws were discovered in a major programming language called PHP, short for Hypertext Preprocessor. Wiz Research calls PHP "the backbone of the web," saying the technology has underpinned much of the internet since the 1990s.

"These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," the firm said, adding that before publicly disclosing the flaw, teams had worked on building a solution that's now available to websites to protect themselves.

As countries scrambled to prevent cyberattacks, numerous websites and pages were taken offline in the past few days. The U.S. National Security Agency warned organizations using PHP to "maintain heightened awareness" over the coming weeks. The U.K.'s National Cyber Security Center called on organizations to "take immediate action" to update their websites to the latest fixed or patched version.

national.title: Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning
national.summary: Recent polls suggest the president is facing challenging headwinds in the state ahead of the midterms.
national.body:
It was just before dawn in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas and the congregation were arriving for the Friday service at the tiny La Lomita Catholic Chapel.

The whitewashed building, which has been here since the days of the American Civil War, rises from the surrounding scrub and sits about 200 yards from the Rio Grande river itself.

As cars pulled up to the chapel, the sound of Father Roy Snipes' barking dogs signalled his arrival. He has been the priest here for almost half a century - and is known locally as the Cowboy Priest.

"I'm not sure why I picked that up, but it's nice," he said of the nickname.

In truth, it is pretty obvious why. Snipes wears a Stetson in place of the more traditional priest's hat. And moments later, the chapel was filled by the sound of a Roy Rogers song - the singer and actor known as the King of the Cowboys.

During the first Trump administration, Snipes resisted plans to seize the chapel's land to build the US president's border wall. Eight years on, at the early Friday service, he focused his short sermon on the actions of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

"There's no good excuse to detain, incarcerate and deport poor, good folks who are our neighbours," Snipes told the congregation of about 30, mainly Hispanic worshippers.

Texas accounted for roughly one-third of all ICE arrests nationwide in July 2026 - a larger share than any other state - according to government figures obtained by the Deportation Data Project.

national.title: Gen Z candidates in both parties aim to tackle high housing costs
national.summary: Young candidates who rent or live with parents say their generation is "in the thick" of the country's housing affordability crisis. They argue this gives them new energy to solve it for everyone.
national.body:
Left: Democrat Olaleye Onikuyide, 28, is running for state representative in Connecticut. Right: Republican Lukas Schubert, 21, is campaigning for reelection as a state representative in Montana. Both candidates are focusing on a lack of affordable housing in their states. Raquel C. Zaldívar and Sarah Mosquera for NPR hide caption

WEST HARTFORD, Conn. — "My bus is running slightly behind," Olaleye Onikuyide texted ahead of our meeting at a coffee shop on West Hartford's main street. The 28-year-old Democrat running for Connecticut state representative still made it on time and said he loved riding public transit.

Family Amid cost-of-living stress, many parents are supporting children well into adulthood Onikuyide also lives with his parents, though he said that's by choice to save money, unlike the many young adults who can't afford to live on their own.

Still, as part of a generation that faces record-high housing unaffordability , he started obsessing years ago over how to make it cheaper. Now that the cripplingly high cost of both rent and homes has become an urgent national conversation, he likens it to being a fan of a niche music group before everyone else caught on.

"All of a sudden, it's blown up and everybody's at the concerts and you're like, 'OK, this is a bit of a crowd here now,'" he said with a broad smile.

Onikuyide and his campaign manager, Karo Shakhnazarov, canvass in West Hartford, Connecticut. Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR hide caption

Nationwide, housing costs are a top issue for voters in a midterms season laser focused on affordability. A chronic housing shortage has pushed up prices, and the fallout cuts across generations.

national.title: Amid Trump's assaults on DEI, how one university is elevating Black students
national.summary: As many colleges roll back or eliminate such programs, Sacramento State has expanded its offerings for students of color.
national.body:
"Black students on our campus are actually showing their faces," says Zyearre Amoah, who works to recruit students in the Black Honors College at Sacramento State. Andri Tambunan for NPR hide caption

When Zyearre Amoah was a student at Sacramento State in 2023, there were times when he felt like the only Black student.

"There were African-American students on our campus," he recalls. But at a sprawling state university with more than 30,000 students, "it just felt like we had to look for each other."

Amoah graduated in 2024, just as his university was launching its Black Honors College, a school within a school with a special focus on Black history, life and culture. He's now a staff member at the BHC, as it's called, helping recruit students.

Criminal Justice Supreme Court upholds pause on Trump's anti-trans prison policy "Unfortunately I didn't have the luxury to be part of it as a student," he says, but the university's effort to elevate, and celebrate, the scholarship of Black students has changed how he perceives his alma mater.

"Black students on our campus are actually showing their faces," he says, laughing. "That is really helpful for everyone here. We're finding each other relatively easier. "

The initiative at Sacramento State, formally known as the California State University, Sacramento, began just months before the Trump administration began its widespread assault on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs on college campuses. In the last two years, dozens of colleges and universities have rolled back or eliminated such offerings to avoid accusations of racial discrimination that have led to loss of research funding and other sanctions.

"Historically, the campus struggled to create an environment of success" for Black students, says Luke Wood, Sac State's president, who helped create the BHC. "So we created an intervention that was designed to meet their needs while also serving any student who was interested in being part of it."

national.title: After nearly 6 years, ex-Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi's son hears her voice
national.summary: Kim Aris tells NPR his mother sounds strong but is in pain. He says she is held at a residence in the capital.
national.body:
In this photo released by Myanmar's government on Thursday, Myanmar's ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi talks on the phone with her son Kim Aris, in Naypyidaw, Myanmar. Myanmar President Spokesperson Office via AP hide caption

CHIANG MAI, Thailand — After nearly six years in detention, Aung San Suu Kyi's first words to her son were a question about his health.

"And then I said all the family was sending their love and asked after her health," said Kim Aris, who spoke by phone with his 81-year-old mother on Thursday, their first direct conversation since the 2021 military coup toppled the democratically elected Myanmar government she led.

The 20-minute call, which Aris, who lives in London, believes the military monitored, offered a rare glimpse of how the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize laureate is being held. She was first sentenced in 2021, with consecutive trials through 2022 bringing her total sentence to 33 years on corruption and electoral fraud charges, widely condemned by the U.S., Western countries, and human rights groups as fabricated. The sentence was later reduced, leaving her with 18 years still to serve.

Little has been known about her condition since the coup, which triggered a civil war that has killed about 100,000 people, according to Armed Conflict Location and Event data, a conflict monitoring organization. The U.N. says the conflict has displaced millions.

In this photo released by Myanmar's government on Thursday, Kim Aris, son of Myanmar's ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi, talks on phone with his mother, at the Myanmar Embassy in London. Myanmar President Spokesperson Office via AP hide caption

"My mother is actually alive and well," said Aris, 49, a carpenter, who has campaigned for her release and sought to raise awareness of the crisis engulfing the Southeast Asian nation. "Hearing her voice has reassured me."

Khaing Khaing Soe, a spokesperson for Myanmar's military-backed president, said on social media that Aris spoke with Suu Kyi by telephone through Myanmar's Embassy in London, and shared separate photographs of the two.

national.title: Hundreds of flights cancelled as Typhoon Champi shuts Taiwan
national.summary: One person has died after being swept away by waves in Taiwan's Liuqiu island, authorities say.
national.body:
Hundreds of flights in the East Asia region were cancelled on Friday as powerful Typhoon Champi roared close to Taiwan's north-east coast.

Schools and offices in Taiwan were shut as Champi neared the island. While it is uncertain if it will make landfall, the storm was forecast to bring 90cm (35in) of rain and strong winds to the north-east until Saturday.

One person died after being swept away by waves, authorities said. The storm also injured 171 people and forced 1,000 others to evacuate.

Champi is the latest in a string of intense typhoons as a Super El Niño heats up the Pacific Ocean and fuels storms. At its peak earlier this week, it was the planet's strongest storm of the year so far.

On Friday afternoon, Champi was packing wind gusts of 191km/h (119mph) .

After passing Taiwan's north-eastern tip and the Okinawa islands in southern Japan, Champi is expected to hover over the waters off China's eastern coast, before curving farther to the north-east to Japan's main island.

Weather agencies in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan forecast that the eye of the storm is expected to pass without making landfall in Taiwan.

However, a forecaster in Taiwan's Central Weather Administration told Reuters that they could not rule this out completely - especially if the storm "stalls, loops or wobbles from side to side" as it approaches.

national.title: Rubio turns to small Indian town as US faces high oil prices
national.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio pushed a business and energy agenda over diplomacy on his second trip to India this year.
national.body:
The western Indian port town of Jamnagar is not a usual stop for foreign leaders, yet it featured prominently in US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's recent visit.

So, why did Rubio visit the town? And, more importantly, why did he skip the Indian capital, Delhi?

The answer to both questions may have less to do with India and more to do with Donald Trump administration's domestic compulsions – or, more precisely, its domestic oil needs.

Rubio arrived in the financial capital Mumbai on Tuesday, where he met Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and some of the country's top business leaders. He officially ended his trip in Jamnagar - in the western state of Gujarat - home to the giant oil refinery owned by one of Asia's richest men, Mukesh Ambani.

It was his second trip to the country this year and experts say what is significant this time is the timing of the visit as well as his choice of destinations.

The Trump administration is under pressure to keep fuel prices in check ahead of November's US midterm elections, while rising tensions in the Middle East threaten global energy supplies.

With little new refining capacity expected in the immediate future in the US, India's ability to process large volumes of crude oil offers Washington a potential way to ease pressure on the fuel markets.

And that puts Reliance's Jamnagar refinery at the centre of the equation.

national.title: Why a student protest movement is challenging 12 years of Vučić rule in Serbia
national.summary: After two years of student protests, Serbians vote on Sunday in elections that could bring down the ruling party.
national.body:
Final campaign rallies have taken place across Serbia, ahead of a snap election billed as a referendum on the country's future.

After two years of student protests, Serbians vote for a new parliament on Sunday in elections that threaten populist leader Aleksandar Vučić's 12 years in power.

The main threat to Vučić's dominance in Serbian politics comes from a two-year-old student movement, but there are concerns surrounding the fairness of the vote.

They have no obvious leaders and are not used to politics, but the "Student List-Students Win" movement has attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.

The Student List is fielding candidates from across Serbian society - and as he joined students marching towards Belgrade, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija Srdanović said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable."

It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people.

The tragedy was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project.

What started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges.

national.title: Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say
national.summary: The quake hit a mountainous, sparsely-populated area in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region.
national.body:
A magnitude 7.0 earthquake has hit a mountainous region in Tibet, killing at least 16 people and injuring dozens, according to Chinese state media.

The centre of the quake hit Baqên County in the Nagqu region on Thursday night, Xinhua reported, citing the local emergency management bureau.

The county - located in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region after annexing it in the 1950s - is 400km (250 miles) north-east of the region's capital, Lhasa.

Authorities have declared the incident an emergency and deployed rescue teams to the affected area, where 65 others have been injured, including 11 people with severe injuries.

The electricity supply has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, though by Friday morning there were reports of power restored in some areas.

Local media said more than 12,400 people had been relocated following the earthquake.

Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas.

The US Geological Survey (USGS) has recorded seven tremors close to the epicentre, all of which are located in the mountainous region. The largest tremor was recorded at 5.2 magnitude at a depth of 10km.

national.summary: It was the biggest earthquake in the region in the last five years, China's national broadcaster CCTV said.
national.body: More than a dozen people were killed and hundreds of homes destroyed when a magnitude 7.0 earthquake hit China's Tibet region on Thursday evening local time, according to local officials.The United States Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10:33 p.m. local time, with its epicenter 119 miles east-northeast of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet. At least 16 people were killed and 54 people were injured in the earthquake, Chinese state media said. Search and rescue efforts continued following the collapse of at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials. Among the injured, 11 people were in serious condition and the other 35 sustained minor injuries, the media office said.More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 1,000 prefabricated housing units, around 3,000 tents and folding beds, as well as flashlights and winter clothing arrived in the region.It was the biggest earthquake in the region in the last five years, China's national broadcaster CCTV said.Nagqu is more than 186 miles north of Tibet's capital, Lhasa.The USGS put the earthquake's depth at 11 miles. Xinhua, citing the China Earthquake Networks Center, put the depth at 6.2 miles. The earthquake comes less than two months after a border region of Nepal and Tibet was struck by devastating flash flooding that left hundreds of people dead and destroyed several communities. Authorities said the flooding was caused by the collapse of a glacier.

national.title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
national.summary: Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave in 2021.
national.body:
A US judge has ordered Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.

The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Trump cancelled a previous deposition - an interview under oath - on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance".

But a lawyer representing the BBC said in court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia that day and had "prioritised that" over answering their questions.

Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is in the phase known as "discovery", in which the two sides provide internal or other records that could form evidence.

Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, told a court in Miami on Thursday that with two months left in the discovery period, Trump had still not completed a deposition.

US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett said Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December or face sanctions - the most extreme of which could be the dismissal of the lawsuit - unless the discovery period is extended.

In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings. Depositions carry legal weight - they are recorded verbatim by a court reporter and the transcripts can later be used as evidence in trials.

national.title: IV team warned Christa Pike's vein might have 'blown' during failed execution, court filing says
national.summary: Tennessee execution team members failed multiple times to establish working IV lines in Christa Pike's arms before her attempted execution and warned that some of her veins may have ruptured, or "blown," before she was injected with the lethal drug, her attorney wrote in a court document filed Thurs
national.body:
Rebecca Boone, Associated Press Rebecca Boone, Associated Press

Kim Chandler, Associated Press Kim Chandler, Associated Press

Tennessee execution team members failed multiple times to establish working IV lines in Christa Pike's arms before her attempted execution and warned that some of her veins may have ruptured, or "blown," before she was injected with the lethal drug, her attorney wrote in a court document filed Thursday.

The IV team went through about 10 needles and tried several IV sites on both arms, attorney Randy Spivey wrote in the document, which provides the most detailed account of the execution attempt so far. They even struggled to push saline through the last IV site they established, Spivey wrote.

Pike, 50, was hospitalized after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 when she tortured and killed Slemmer with her boyfriend, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death.

State protocol calls for a second dose of pentobarbital if the first doesn't result in death, but it doesn't spell out what to do if a person survives the second injection.

After being taken to a hospital, Pike was on a ventilator for several days. At one point, her attorneys did not expect her to survive. She ultimately regained consciousness and returned to prison after being discharged.

The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences. The court document was part of a separate legal proceeding in which people on the state's death row are challenging Tennessee's lethal injection procedures.

And they're not the only ones concerned.Flock advertises itself as a camera system designed to help authorized users find relevant evidence for investigations without compromising safety and compliance. Their features include recording vehicle sightings at a specific place and time, and capturing license plates and vehicle characteristics.However, the tech has become a hot-button issue for municipalities across the country. A Reuters-Ipsos poll conducted in August found that Americans are mixed on having the technology in their communities. According to the study, Americans ages 55 and up, and a majority of Republicans of all ages, support the use of Flock technologies, while only 21% of Americans 18 to 34 support their installation.Additionally, unease around the tech has grown as more and more stories come to light about alleged misuse by law enforcement. Last week, three Cheektowaga police employees were suspended for misusing Flock camera data, but will not face criminal charges.Currently, there are 13 Flock cameras between Fredonia and Dunkirk. local.title: Collection that showcases Rochester's Puerto Rican history is being preserved
local.summary: The University of Rochester's Department of Rare Books, Special Collection and Preservation acquired a collection from Henry Ignacio Padrón-Morales, a longtime activist, educator, musician and poet.
local.body:
Decades of work documenting Rochester's Puerto Rican community, arts collaborations and bilingual education are now preserved in a University of Rochester archive.

The collection belongs to Henry Ignacio Padrón-Morales , a longtime activist, educator, musician and poet who moved to Rochester as a teenager in the late 1960s and became a leader in Rochester's Latino community.

"I have grown more accepting of the fact that Rochester is my home," Padrón-Morales said. "I'm from here. I am from here. I've given this place a chunk of my life, and that is important in and of itself to have had that growth because I'll talk to people and you know they're from here, they're everywhere, but after being here this long, I consider Rochester as my home."

Over the years, Padrón-Morales has worn many different hats in Rochester, working as an educator in the Rochester City School District, a community advocate, and most recently co-owner of Hipocampo Children's Bookstore .

His work documenting the city's Puerto Rican community and its cultural and educational history is now in the care of the University of Rochester's Department of Rare Books, Special Collections and Preservation. The university acquired his documents for its archives, cataloging them as the "Henry I. Padrón-Morales papers."

The collection documents Padrón-Morales' work as an activist, organizer, artist, collaborator, volunteer and advocate for Puerto Rico and Rochester's Latino community.

"I was like gripping it, like you know, not out of total distrust, but out of some distrust in what would happen with it. How would it be treated? And not today, as I've seen, it's in a good beginning stage, and in good hands," Padrón-Morales told WXXI News.

Conversations about archiving his work began in 2025 when Molly Ball, associate professor of history at the University of Rochester, applied for a historic preservation grant through the Rochester Area Community Foundation.

local.title: Greece schools seek sustainable solutions to meet vulnerable students' needs
local.summary: The Greece Central School District is looking for long term solutions to meet a growing need for specialized instruction for students.
local.body:
Listen • 1:08 The Greece Central School District is looking for long term solutions to meet a growing need for specialized instruction for students.

Assistant Superintendent Michael Zaffuts outlined three key areas of need — space for special education instruction, funding for a program designed for vulnerable students — for instance who have mental illness diagnoses, low grades, or are chronically absent — and adjustments to account for shifting enrollment at schools.

"These long-standing challenges led us to a place where we felt like we needed a long-term systemic effort to try to tackle them to represent not only solutions to those problems but also what our community values and matching a solution to those and a path forward with what our community values," Zaffuts said at a school board meeting Tuesday.

Special education enrollment at Greece schools is up by about 150 students compared with five years ago.

"We currently have services being delivered in hallways and cafeterias on a regular basis, and we need to figure out what is a long-term and viable solution to support those students and staff members," Zaffuts said, referring to the increased enrollment of students who need specialized instruction.

The district's Alcott Road campus is also in need of long-term financial support he said. The campus houses programs like Phoenix Academy which provides trauma-sensitive support for high schoolers, GED classes, and tutoring.

The district is working with consultants at Leadership Solutions Advisors to find potential solutions. The school board expects to hear about next steps on Dec. 1, followed by a presentation of three possible pathways by June.

"It's a huge undertaking, and it's something that everyone will have to kind of adjust in certain ways," School board member Mary Lyke said. "But I think for the district in the long run, it's just such a healthy thing to do."

local.title: With lockout looming, World Series could be last games for a while
local.summary: MILWAUKEE — On the eve of the World Series, there is a realization these may be Major League Baseball’s last games for a while. Owners are pushing for a salary cap, and that could prompt a lockout starting Dec. 2 and result in canceled games in 2027. “It would be a real bummer to lose […]
local.body:
MILWAUKEE -- On the eve of the World Series, there is a realization these may be Major League Baseball’s last games for a while.

Owners are pushing for a salary cap, and that could prompt a lockout starting Dec. 2 and result in canceled games in 2027.

“It would be a real bummer to lose a season, that’s for sure,” Tampa Bay ace Drew Rasmussen said Thursday ahead of the World Series opener against Milwaukee. “I think the industry as a whole is in way too good of a place.”

This year’s World Series is the first since 1991 between teams both in the bottom half of payrolls: Milwaukee ranked 19th as of Aug. 31 and Tampa Bay 25th. MLB says a cap is needed to help all teams compete more consistently, but players contend because of the method owners use to define expenses, a cap would lead to management taking a greater share of the sport’s revenue.

“The system that’s being proposed, which is similar to other leagues in terms of revenue-sharing system, not only will help us compete, but more importantly all of the teams with lower payrolls, too, which is something also I think the fans want,” Brewers owner Mark Attanasio said.

MLB’s proposal would cap spending in 2027 at $245.3 million using figures for luxury tax payrolls, and limit a player to 15% of a team’s payroll. Free agents would be capped at $265 million over six seasons -- far under Juan Soto’s record $765 million, 15-year deal with the New York Mets.

“If they’re going to sit there and wave their little magic wand at us saying they’re going to get a salary cap, it’s not going to happen,” Brewers pitcher Trevor Megill said.

Negotiations for a collective bargaining agreement to replace the five-year deal expiring Dec. 1 could turn into each side trying to outlast the other.

local.title: Silver Creek receives clean audit report
local.summary: SILVER CREEK — The Silver Creek Central School District received a clean, unmodified opinion of its finances in an Independent Audit Report through the end of last school year. The district discussed the results of the report at a recent Board of Education meeting. The report was conducted by certif
local.body:
SILVER CREEK -- The Silver Creek Central School District received a clean, unmodified opinion of its finances in an Independent Audit Report through the end of last school year. The district discussed the results of the report at a recent Board of Education meeting.

The report was conducted by certified public accountants Buffamante, Whipple, Buttafaro, for the period ending June 30. Matt Miller, Business Office Manager, was commended for his work by the Board and Superintendent Dr. Katie Ralston, who said the positive report is "truly an accomplishment".

The district was, however, cited for having far too much money deemed as unassigned fund balance. As a result, a corrective action plan was required to address the district's unassigned funds of $6,537,152, which equates to approximately 19.6% of the 2026-27 school budget. The state legal limit is 4%, but districts across the state often exceed that figure. Silver Creek's unassigned fund balance in the previous year's report was roughly 15%.

Ralston clarified the excess fund balance is not unused tax revenue or "extra money" the district has at its disposal. Rather, it is what she called a "complicated calculation" of budget transfers regarding money allocated to the district's 2024 Capital Project. While the project was approved in 2024, the invoices for the work come in as the work is done, meaning the funds must be available to pay the bills throughout the project.

Ralston said the amount of unassigned fund balance "is not because it can be used for anything that we want it to be. It is not because we are squirreling away money. It is because it's a very designated and intentional use for our Capital Improvement Project and our vehicle purchases."

The $36.1 million Capital Project is the largest Capital Project in the school's history. The project was fully funded through capital reserves and state aid reimbursement, resulting in no tax increase to residents. Approximately $5.8 million of reserve funds were moved between accounts to cover Capital Project costs. A capital reserve fund was dissolved, resulting in additional revenue to the district.

The report also found no compliance issues or any general control issues in its single audit of the district's Impact Aid funds. A single audit was required due to the amount of federal funds received by the district this past year.

Also at the recent meeting, Desiree Clarke was appointed as Internal Claims Auditor for the remainder of the 2026-27 school year. Kelly Imhoff was provisionally appointed as a 12-month Clerk II at a rate of $16.25 per hour. Brookelynn Wood resigned as a 10-Month Cleaner.

local.body:
Fredonia has hired a real estate firm to appraise the value of three unused parcels in the town of Pomfret.

During the recent Village Board meeting, trustees approved a resolution to authorize Amy Holt of Holt Appraisals to perform the appraisal on the Glasgow Road properties for $1,000.

Earlier this year, village officials had discussed selling the land to help "ease the financial burden" of the village.

"I do want to remind the board that we have a verbal commitment to a real estate company, once those appraisals come through," Fredonia Mayor Michael Ferguson said following the resolution's approval.

County map records show the village presently owns approximately 43 acres of land on Upper Cassadaga Lake which was called Glasgow Park. Even though it has "park" in the name, it is not a formal park, with signage, posted hours or designated trails.

Last fall, the village board rejected a resolution to sell the property, requesting more time to investigate the proposal. Among those who voted no were Trustees Ben Brauchler and Paul Wandel, both who supported Monday's resolution.

At the beginning of the year, when two new trustees were seated, the proposal was reexamined by Trustee LeeAnn Lazarony.

After she brought it up in February, a number of residents protested the sale of the property, saying they didn't want to see it be sold for commercial development.

OBSERVER Photo by Christian Storms Randolph's Jaydan Champlin, right, celebrates his goal with Tanner Patterson during the first half against Portville in the Section VI Class C quarterfinals on Thursday at Allegany-Limestone High School.

OBSERVER Photo by Christian Storms Randolph's Isaac Pihlblad, right, battles with Portville's Colin German for possession during the Section VI Class C quarterfinals at Allegany-Limestone High School on Thursday.

ALLEGANY -- After leveling the score in the 64th minute, Portville continued its relentless attack toward the Randolph goal seeking the winner in the Section VI Class C boys soccer quarterfinals.

Watching Tanner Patterson's free kick sail into the Portville box during the 71st minute, Randolph senior Gavin Senn patiently waited for his moment and, after Grady Steward knocked the ball out of the scrum, Senn made his move with a quick strike that put the Cardinals ahead for good, 2-1 on Thursday night at Allegany-Limestone High School.

"The wind was definitely a factor," Randolph head coach Dave Pihlblad stated. "We had to go into it in the second half with a 1-0 lead and Portville was all over us for the first 15-20 minutes of the half. They got that goal and deep down inside I didn't have a good feeling because we weren't creating and they were all over us. Then just one moment, it's in the back of the net and we held on for dear life the last 10 minutes there."

The Cardinals regained the lead less than 10 minutes after Portville's Colin German leveled the score at 1-1, finishing a great run shooting back to the left while dribbling past the Randolph defense. With Portville already in control of the momentum much of the second half, German's goal tipped the scales even further and the Cardinals looked to be hanging on for overtime.

Instead, it was Randolph getting that next goal and the Cardinals really put the pressure on their Chautauqua-Cattaraugus Athletic Association Division II rival to score again in the final nine minutes.

local.body:
It's too soon to call what happened this week to artificial intelligence stocks a correction. Call it instead a reminder: Hype about new technologies is an inevitable human temptation, and sometimes it pays off, but eventually investors demand returns on capital.

That's the way to think about the disconcerting market swings of recent days. Many tech shares have taken a dive, sometimes by large percentages. That has dragged down the NASDAQ and the S&P 500 index, which has come to be dominated by those companies. Our advice is to go for a relaxing walk this weekend instead of checking your 401(k) balance.

This seems counterintuitive in the face of encouraging earnings reports from some big AI-related companies, and in some cases the good earnings news arrested the decline in the company's stock price. But stock prices are forward rather than backward looking, and investors still are grappling with big questions about the AI future.

AI will have a profound effect on the global economy. It remains impossible to say what those effects might be or who will profit from them, and how. Estimates of global AI-related investments regularly top $1 trillion per year and probably are undercounts after including other forms of investment such as the companies that adopt AI in their own businesses.

This implies that AI would need to substantially boost business productivity and generate unprecedented returns eventually. One recent academic study calculated that American data-center hyperscalers alone would need to earn revenue equal to roughly 9% of gross domestic product per year by 2032 to break even on their investments.

America's ability to raise and allocate this private capital--the institutional investors and entrepreneurs, the legal system and market structure--is the envy of the world. But unforgiving market discipline on the way down is a not-so-secret ingredient in the special sauce.

As AI continues to evolve, the challenge will be to reevaluate the risks and do so relative to other bets. It's a continuous process that plays out every second markets are open.

Investors this week didn't abandon equities entirely, even if they did pour some capital back into the bond market. Instead, they pivoted into recently overlooked industries such as consumer goods. The Dow Jones Industrial Average had a decent week.

local.title: Chautauqua Co. Amish school at center of vaccine case that could go to Supreme Court
local.summary: A legal battle over school vaccine requirements is unfolding in Western New York, where an Amish school is at the center of a case that could reach the U.S. Supreme Court for a second time.
local.body: A legal battle over school vaccine requirements is unfolding in Western New York, where an Amish school in Chautauqua County is at the center of a case that could reach the U.S. Supreme Court for a second time.The case challenges New York's decision to eliminate religious exemptions from school vaccination requirements. It has to do with physical health and safety. It's neutral on its face. It applies to everyone. It has nothing to do with the free exercise of religion," Macomber said.The lawsuit first went before a federal judge in the Western District of New York. She ruled against the Amish plaintiffs, citing legal precedent upholding a similar vaccine requirement in Connecticut.The plaintiffs appealed to the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, which also ruled against them.They then asked the U.S. Supreme Court to take up the case. local.title: Niagara Falls continues Main Street revitalization; unveils Niagara University housing plan
local.summary: Niagara Falls unveiled plans to turn a Main Street building that has been vacant for decades into Niagara University student housing, as plans to revitalize dozens of properties in the corridor continue.
local.body: Niagara Falls unveiled plans to turn a Main Street building that has been vacant for decades into Niagara University student housing, as plans to revitalize dozens of properties in the corridor continue.For decades, several blocks of Main Street in Niagara Falls have been left to rot, but in 2024, plans were announced to redevelop several long-forgotten buildings.WATCH: Niagara Falls continues Main Street revitalization; unveils Niagara University housing plan“It’s not going to be the Main Street of our childhood. It’s going to be better,” Mayor Robert Restaino said in 2024.He and the City of Niagara Falls acquired 38 Main Street properties, between Ontario Avenue and Michigan Avenue, from absentee landlords to resell them to new developers through incentivized deals. Restaino said the city has made deals for a little less than half of the 38 total properties. These properties carry so many memories for residents, like Jenss Department Store or The Rapids Theater.“I would say we are at least in the 20s of properties we still have that we’re looking to develop,” Restaino said. “And now, what was the initial, I would say, linchpin or centerpiece of what we hope to do on Main Street is happening.”The centerpiece that he referred to is 2018 and 2010 Main Street, a building that has been boarded up since, at the very least, 2007.Developer Abe Bose announced plans to invest $25 million into the building to transform it into Niagara University student housing. He said that it would host 100 units of student housing and commercial space.“It’s not just about replacing blighted structures with modern, premium student housing and ground-floor retail. It’s about creating an economic engine that brings foot traffic and daily activity back to this block,” Bose said.While that is a nice addition, Restaino hopes it will be a catalyst to find even more developers.“Collectively, there’s in excess of $50 million of private investment here,” Restaino said.Projects underway include both market rate apartments and commercial buildings. They have various completion dates, but Restaino hopes to see the Niagara University housing open late 2028.Join the Niagara County Community News Facebook group to connect with neighbors and learn about what's happening in your community.

local.title: Buffalo voters to decide 11 proposed city charter changes
local.summary: Beyond the candidates on the ballot, Buffalo voters will also decide on 11 proposed changes to the City of Buffalo Charter.
local.body: Beyond the candidates on the ballot, Buffalo voters will also decide on 11 proposed changes to the City of Buffalo Charter.A sample ballot shows the 11 charter questions take up about a third of the front of the ballot and the entire back.The City Charter essentially serves as the rulebook for Buffalo city government, outlining how it operates and what it can and cannot do.Laurence Rubin, chairman of the City of Buffalo Charter Revision Commission, said the proposals allow residents to have a say in how their local government operates.“It's important because it's giving the citizens of Buffalo an opportunity to speak about their constitution, their local constitution,” Rubin said. WATCH: Buffalo voters to decide 11 proposed city charter changesThe Buffalo Common Council created the Charter Revision Commission and held public hearings to discuss and fine-tune the proposed changes.Rubin said many of the questions examined by the commission were prompted by issues that surfaced when Chris Scanlon took over as acting mayor following Byron Brown's departure.“There were issues like, is he really the acting mayor or just has the powers of a mayor, and what happened to his council seat,” Rubin said. But the proposed changes go well beyond questions surrounding mayoral succession and cover a wide range of issues involving city government.“It affects everything from how they participate in voting, to how the budget is made, to how citizens participate in advisory boards, to issues like how the police are serving the community, to dealing with issues about whether or not human rights are being affected in the City of Buffalo,” Rubin said.Early voting starts Saturday. Voters interested in learning more about each of the 11 proposed charter changes can review more information from the City of Buffalo Charter Revision Commission. The city's commission page includes information designed to help understand the proposals.Rubin said he hopes voters turn out and make their voices heard on the questions found on the back of the ballot.“I would hope that people will vote. I hope people come out and vote in general, right? That's our civic duty, and I hope they flip the page and vote for everything,” Rubin said.

local.title: City of Buffalo releases 2026-2027 Winter Snow Plan
local.summary: The City of Buffalo has released its 2026-2027 Winter Snow Plan, including $2.7 million for contracted snow removal, new equipment to help clear narrow side streets, and upgraded snowplow tracking.
local.body: The City of Buffalo has released its 2026-2027 Winter Snow Plan, including $2.7 million for contracted snow removal, new equipment to help clear narrow side streets of snow and upgraded snowplow tracking. "Buffalo residents deserve reliable service on their streets, and being better prepared for winter is a big part of fixing the basics," Mayor Sean Ryan said. "We are putting more resources behind snow removal and investing in equipment tailored to our city’s needs. We are also giving our crews the tools and resources they need to work more efficiently. These are practical improvements to help people get where they need to go and keep our neighborhoods accessible when winter weather arrives."The plan also calls for at least one plow pass on every residential street within 24 hours of snowfall. Crews would first focus on major roads, emergency access routes and bus routes before turning to neighborhoods. The Ryan administration submitted its first snow plan more than 200 days after the April 1 deadline. But Deputy Mayor Benjamin Swanekamp told 7 News snow removal plans have been a priority for the Ryan administration since they came into office."Not a week has gone by that I haven't had some meeting where we're investigating how to improve snow removal services," Swanekamp said. "We've been working on iterating on this for a long time, and it's going to be ready before the council, well before any snow hits the ground." 7 News gained exclusive access to the Broadway Barns as final preparations for winter are underway, with the city already set if a mild or moderate winter storm hits, according to Swanekamp. entertainment.title: ‘She’s My Muse’: Adéla Lost It When Nicole Kidman Mentioned Her on Late-Night TV
entertainment.summary: The rising Slovak pop star made her TV debut on "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon" with an interview and performance of “Nicole Kidman” and “Ain't In LA.”
entertainment.body:
Never meet your heroes. That is unless you’re Adéla and your hero is Nicole Kidman, then go for gold.

With two songs on the Billboard Hot 100 right now, Adéla is having a real moment, and she’s waving the flag for her homeland, Slovakia.

If it all feels unreal, bizarre even, Adéla can be forgiven. Ever since she learned to read and write, her mind has been occupied with the American dream . As a youngster, the Disney Channel was constantly switched on at the family home, Adéla hatched a plan and a timeline.

“I basically wanted to be famous,” she told Jimmy Fallon, when she stopped by NBC ’s The Tonight Show for Thursday night’s episode. Her education included watching Fallon’s interviews with Ariana Grande, Miley Cyrus and others. Explore Adéla See latest videos, charts and news

Dreams, they sometimes come true. Adéla boasts a top 10 hit with the viral song “Nicole Kidman,” lifting 9-6 on the latest Billboard Hot 100 , for a new high. A month ago, when Kidman stopped by The Tonight Show , conversation quickly moved to Adéla and her ode to the Australian actress. “I can’t believe it. She wrote a song called ‘Nicole Kidman,’” the Oscar winner remarked at the time . “She’s so talented.” Related Tate McRae Debuts at No. 1 In Australia With 'Housewife' LISA, Miley, Kacey Musgraves & John Mayer: New Music Friday Guide Cristian Castro Accepts the Billboard Lifetime Achievement Award 'In the Name of Romantic Love'

Deep breath, Adéla. “That’s too much to even think about,” she explained to Fallon. “She’s my muse.” Kidman, well “she’s doing charity work by mentioning my name all over town. It’s amazing.”

If that was strange, Adéla must’ve felt like she entered Weirdworld when Kidman, Dua Lipa, Pedro Pascal and other a-listers created TikToks to Adéla’s music. “I was like, this is not real. I’m being pranked obviously, I honestly thought it was AI. But it was not,” she recounted in her late-night interview.

Adéla’s mom is, of course, on her side, freaking out just like her daughter. “She also loves Nicole,” the rising pop star admitted. “She was beside herself. She was like ‘I don’t know if people are going crazy of if you’re a genius. But it’s working.’”

entertainment.title: Judge Orders Trump to Testify Under Oath in BBC Defamation Lawsuit
entertainment.summary: The President could face sanctions if he fails to answer questions by the December deadline.
entertainment.body:
Logo text A U.S. judge has told Donald Trump that he must answer questions in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC or face sanctions.

If the President does not sit for a deposition under oath by Dec. 11, the most extreme outcome might include the dismissal of the entire suit, according to the BBC .

Last year, Trump sued the British broadcaster over claims that a BBC Panorama documentary was doctored to make it appear as though Trump, during his Jan. 6, 2021 speech outside the White House, had urged his followers to attack the Capitol. Related Stories Business Nobody Knew This Game Existed, and Now It's a Hot 2027 Title TV 'MobLand' EP Teases What Season 3 Holds for Tom Hardy as 'Laird' Star Peter Sarsgaard Shares How He Feels About Playing a "Malevolent U.S. Billionaire"

The 33-page document, brought in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida last December, alleges that the BBC made “a false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction of President Trump.”

A BBC spokesperson told The Hollywood Reporter as news of the lawsuit broke: “While the BBC sincerely regrets the manner in which the video clip was edited, we strongly disagree [that] there is a basis for a defamation claim.”

Ten months later, Trump cancelled a previous deposition set for Oct. 16, citing “matters of national importance.” A lawyer for the BBC said in court that Trump was actually campaigning in Georgia and had “prioritized that” over answering questions.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett said Trump must sit for the deposition by Dec. 11 or he’ll face sanctions, unless this “discovery period” — described by the BBC as the phase where both sides provide internal or other records that could form evidence — is extended.

All of this came about when a leaked BBC memo from an independent advisor, a man named Michael Prescott, concluded that the doc Trump: A Second Chance? “seemed to be taking a distinctly anti-Trump stance.”

entertainment.title: ‘Apart,’ Set in Cyprus and Apartheid South Africa, “Challenges the Idea of ‘Us’ and ‘Them'” (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer)
entertainment.summary: Writer-director Stelana Kliris’ feature, starring Leem Lubany and Luca Pasqualino and inspired by the experiences of her refugee parents, will open PÖFF’s Critics’ Picks section.
entertainment.body:
Can a young woman forced to leave a divided Cyprus in the 1970s find belonging and even love in an arranged marriage in Apartheid South Africa, especially when a secret from her past threatens to change everything? With Apart , South African Cypriot writer-director Stelana Kliris ( Find Me Falling , Committed ) has created a deeply personal film about displacement, belonging, borders, both the ones that are physical and those that are in our hearts, and human connections. And it is inspired by the real experiences of her refugee parents.

The movie, world-premiering at the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF), stars Leem Lubany ( Omar , Rock the Kasbah ), Luca Pasqualino ( Rivals , The Musketeers ) and Girley Jazama ( Under the Hanging Tree , The White Line ). Related Stories Movies 'Biermann' Director Explains Why His Doc About a German Political Singer Is a Film for the Trump Era Business Nobody Knew This Game Existed, and Now It's a Hot 2027 Title

“In 1974, when Turkey invades Cyprus, young Eleni (Lubany) leaves her homeland through an arranged marriage and finds herself in Apartheid South Africa, swapping one divided country for another,” reads a synopsis for the film. “There, a new life with Nico (Pasqualino) slowly turns into love, until an unexpected friendship forces her to confront a secret from her past.”

Shot in Cyprus with a story that goes between Cyprus and South Africa, Apart brings a turbulent time in the 1970s to life, with a focus on a female perspective. The filmmaker’s Find Me Falling became the first Cypriot film to premiere on Netflix.

Apart will open Tallinn’s Critics’ Picks section. “With this very personal and ambitious film, Stelana Kliris has delivered a deeply moving cinematic ode to humanity, a film that will stay with you long after the final frame,” the festival website teases.

With cinematography by Simon Sarketzis and editing by Emilios Avraam, Apart is being sold by Reinvent Yellow Sales. The producers are Kliris, Susan Simnett, Jamie Harvey and Ioanna Bolomyti.

“It has always fascinated me that people like my parents, who emigrated from Cyprus to South Africa, left one divided place for another, and I wanted to translate this into a film that challenges the idea of ‘us’ and ‘them,’ and, whilst the central narrative is fictional, the individual events around it are from real events,” Kliris says. “This is an intimate, character-driven film with a specific set of aesthetics that represents not just the two locations, but two distinct periods, 1970s South Africa interwoven with flashbacks to the Cypriot past, and while war and Apartheid serve as the backdrop, our story of love, friendship and identity provides for a more human, intimate experience.”

entertainment.title: Ryan Gosling’s Band Dead Man’s Bones Announces Comeback With New Music
entertainment.summary: After 17 years, Gosling and Zach Shields are reviving their rock duo.
entertainment.body:
Barbie offered up a taste of rock star Ryan Gosling , but now there’s more on the way.

Dead Man’s Bones, the rock duo comprised of Gosling and Zach Shields, announced on the band’s Instagram on Thursday that new music is coming Oct. 27. The pair put out their first and only album, a self-titled collaboration with the Silverlake Conservatory Children’s Choir, in 2009, and 17 years later it appears it’s time for a comeback.

Gosling and Shields were known for their spooky sound, with songs that centered on ghosts and monsters. They appear to be sticking to that theme with their Halloween-season return, as the announcement video features a haunting man telling the viewer, “Dead man’s bones must wait to rise, from the house where shadows cry. All of this must change Oct. 27, when our ghosts must leave our world for this, to dance with us at twilight time, and bring your hand to lie in mine.” The voice of a young girl — likely one of Gosling’s two daughters — yells the release date. Related Stories Movies Austin Abrams Still Won't Admit Which Was Tougher to Shoot, 'Whalefall' or 'Resident Evil' Lifestyle You Want Those Tattoos From 'The Bear'? Call Benny Shields

Gosling’s partner Eva Mendes had begun to recently tease the band’s return, posting on her page, “Trying to summon new music from Dead Man’s Bones” and then following the confirmation, she wrote, “He came through on his promise to me.”

Though the group has been dormant for years, Gosling has showed off his singing chops in La La Land and Barbie , earning a Grammy nomination for the latter with his performance of “I’m Just Ken.” He famously brought down the house with a live performance of the song at the Oscars in 2024.

The music adds to a very busy time of life for star, who is in the middle of an Oscar campaign for Project Hail Mary and has Star Wars: Starfighter coming out next year, along with Marvel’s Ghost Rider also on the horizon.

entertainment.body:
Fuerza Regida was the big winner at the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards, sweeping eight awards during the ceremony Thursday night (Oct. 22) at the James L. Knight Center in Miami, FL.

The Música Mexicana sensation’s big night included Hot Latin Song of the Year; Streaming Song of the Year; Global 200 Latin Song of the Year; Regional Mexican Song of the Year; Hot Latin Songs Artist of the Year, Duo or Group; Top Latin Albums Artist of the Year, Duo or Group; and Regional Mexican Artist of the Year, Duo or Group.

The Latin favorites also won the Billboard Vanguard Award for their innovative and creative vision. Other special award recipients this year included Cristian Castro who was honored with the Billboard Lifetime Achievement Award, Rosalía with the Hall of Fame Award, and Rubén Blades with the Billboard Icon Award.

“I wouldn’t be able to do what I do if it weren’t for the artists who came before me and paved the way—artists like him, whom I admire so much. Celia Cruz, Rocío, Vicente Fernandez, Daddy Yankee…it is incredible to be receiving this today,” Rosalía said during her speech. “And last but certainly not least, thank you to Latin America for the place you’ve given me, and for all these years of inspiration and lessons. I hope to keep finding ways to return all that affection and generosity to you. Here’s to many more years — thank you!”

Ahead of all the glitz and glamor that beamed out on Telemundo and Peacock, Billboard’s Ingrid Fajardo and Jessica Roiz hosted a livestream on the blue carpet, where many exciting and behind-the-scenes moments were captured.

Before kicking off the evening with the performance of his new single “La Gozadera en Navidad” alongside Elvis Crespo, Victor Manuelle brought the party to the blue carpet. There, the one-time finalist talked about his holiday traditions which are reflected in his new holiday album that includes collaborations with Gilberto Santa Rosa, Tito Nieves, José Alberto “El Canario,” and many more.

To further get us in the Christmas spirit, the Puerto Rican singer invited rising group BLB to spice up the livestream with a fun plena tune.

Focus track “Tarantino” packs just as hard a punch , while “Cobra” is an attitude-packed dance-pop song and album closer “Sweat” is a sultry song that leaves its subject with a simple instruction — “don’t stress me out” — and its listener wanting more. Press Play follows the 2025 release of LISA’S debut solo full-length, Alter Ego , and arrives just in time for the Thai singer’s upcoming Vegas residency that kicks off in November. — LYNDSEY HAVENS

For longtime Miley fans, the release of “Cold Blooded” has been a long time coming. Written in the late 2010s ahead of her EP She Is Coming , the track never saw the light of day — until now. A demo version of the ballad, which showcases Miley’s undeniable vocal control and power over simple piano chords, is featured as a bonus track on the season three soundtrack for Nobody Wants This , out today. Its one of two Miley demos that made it on the album, as a stripped-down version of her Endless Summer Vacation track “You” also features on the soundtrack and in an episode. The soundtrack is out on Atlantic, while all 10 episodes of season three are now streaming on Netflix. — L . H.

Kacey Musgraves is previewing her upcoming project Middle of Nowhere Vol. 2: Tex Mex Tapes (out Jan. 15 on Lost Highway Records) with the release of new music, including “Weekend In Texas.” “I’ve got the hat and the cattle to back it up / Everything will be great in my favorite state of mind,” she sings. Bright horns, an irresistible groove and Musgraves’ dulcet vocal tones blend luxuriously as she sings of longing for a soul-restoring few days of escape in the Lone Star State. This new release feels both classic and invigorating. — JESSICA NICHOLSON

entertainment.title: Cristian Castro Accepts the Billboard Lifetime Achievement Award ‘In the Name of Romantic Love’
entertainment.summary: The pop icon also performed at the Thursday (Oct. 22) ceremony, broadcasted live on Telemundo.
entertainment.body:
Cristian Castro became emotional on Thursday evening (Oct. 22) as he accepted the Billboard Lifetime Achievement Award at the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards , delivering a poetic speech inspired by love.

“Romantic love and poetry are the only real things — the truest aspects of our human existence, the firmest thought, the clearest expression that emerges from our spirit and our hearts from the time we are children,” the pop icon remarked upon receiving the award from Mexican actress Jacqueline Bracamontes. “It is like when we first behold the soul — the serene calm of morning dew, the Moon, the majesty of a sunset — and that face, that presence, which fills your entire soul and which you cannot cast out from your being.”

“Throughout my life, romantic love has been my focal point and my true ambition — my firmament and my greatest longing,” continued the singer behind No. 1 hits such as “Amor” and “Azul.” “I accept this award in the name of romantic love and in the name of poetry; they are the most beautiful things I have ever possessed — gifts placed within me by God, alongside my voice.”

Castro, who received the honor in recognition of a glittering career spanning more than three decades and his enduring influence on Latin music, also took to the stage for a special performance during the ceremony, broadcast live on Telemundo and Peacock from the James L. Knight Center in Miami. Together with the Mexican-American duo Ha*Ash, he performed their new collaboration “Antes Que Te Cases” live for the first time.

The Billboard Lifetime Achievement Award honors an artist for an exceptional professional career — someone who has elevated Latin music to a new level on the global stage, remains relevant through their artistic and personal contributions, and whose influence has shaped the development of Latin music worldwide. Previous recipients include Andrea Bocelli, Armando Manzanero, Carlos Santana, José José, Maná, Marco Antonio Solís, Ricardo Arjona and Roberto Carlos, among others.

Castro has solidified his place as one of the defining voices of Latin pop and romantic music. His history on the Billboard charts began in 1992 when “No Podrás” became his first entry on Hot Latin Songs, reaching No. 3. His debut album, Agua Nueva , climbed to No. 2 on Top Latin Pop Albums in January 1993. Since then, he has achieved six No. 1s on Hot Latin Songs, including “Nunca Voy a Olvidarte,” “Amor” and “Azul,” which spent four, eleven and nine weeks at the top, respectively. Years later, Viva El Príncipe , his tribute to legendary Mexican singer José José, spent seven weeks at No. 1 on Top Latin Albums in 2011.
